response: ## The finding ``` crime_00037 · oversized_raster · "Oversized Raster" · severity low · confidence 0.95 src/assets/hero-banner.png byte size: 260,000 bytes (253.9 KB) severity ladder: low ≥ 200 KB · medium ≥ 500 KB · high ≥ 1000 KB format: png ``` ## Verdict: request changes, don't block 254 KB sits on the bottom rung of the ladder — it clears the 200 KB floor by ~27% and is nowhere near the 500 KB medium or 1 MB high thresholds. It's also the lowest-ranked finding in the whole report (`agent_risk` 0.14, `effort: quick`), and it carries no correctness risk: nothing breaks, nothing silently misbehaves. What keeps it from being a rubber-stamp is *where* it lands. A landing-page hero is almost always the LCP element, so those 260 KB are on the critical path for the site's most-measured page. A quarter-megabyte PNG is roughly a second of LCP on a mid-tier connection. That's worth one round of changes, not a merge veto. So: comment, request the re-encode, approve on the follow-up push. If the team runs a performance budget in CI, this is the case for wiring one up rather than for holding the branch hostage. ## The transformation **One caveat first:** the finding reports bytes but not intrinsic dimensions — `oversized_raster` triggers on size alone (contrast `crime_00036`, where the icon detector does report `32 × 32`). So confirm the actual pixel dimensions and the CSS render width before picking targets; the numbers below are the standard hero shape, not measurements of this file. **Dimensions.** Don't ship one image. Generate a `srcset` at 640 / 960 / 1280 / 1920 px wide and let the browser pick: ```html ``` 1920 px is the right ceiling for a full-bleed hero: it covers a 1920 desktop at 1x and a 960-px container at 2x. Going past that buys nothing visible — cap DPR at 2x rather than shipping a 3x asset. Keep explicit `width`/`height` so the hero doesn't cause CLS, `fetchpriority="high"` because it's the LCP element, and **no** `loading="lazy"` — lazy-loading the LCP image actively hurts the metric. Budget: **≤ 100 KB for the largest variant**, which puts every variant well under the detector's 200 KB floor and stops this finding recurring. **Format: AVIF primary, WebP fallback.** For a photographic hero, AVIF typically lands 30–50% smaller than WebP at perceptually equal quality (`-q 50`–`60` in `avifenc`/`cavif` is usually indistinguishable from the PNG), and this is precisely the asset where those bytes convert into an LCP improvement. Support is universal across current Chrome, Firefox, Safari 16+, and Edge; the `` fallback covers the residual tail at zero risk. Two reasons to reach for WebP instead: - **The hero has baked-in text or crisp UI edges.** AVIF's chroma handling smears fine high-frequency detail at aggressive quality settings. If the banner is artwork with type in it, either raise the AVIF quality or ship WebP alone. - **The build can't absorb the encode cost.** AVIF encoding is an order of magnitude slower than WebP. If assets are encoded per-CI-run rather than committed, that shows up in build times. If the team wants exactly one format and no `` plumbing, take WebP — simpler, universally supported, still 25–35% off the PNG for photographic content. The underlying mistake worth naming in the review comment: **PNG is the wrong codec for a photographic hero.** It's lossless, which is what you want for screenshots and flat-color UI, and what you're paying a large premium for on a photograph. If the banner is actually flat-color or gradient artwork, the better answer may be no raster at all — an SVG or a CSS gradient, per the finding's own `shrink_raster` action. ## One thing adjacent to this PR The same directory holds `crime_00032` — `src/assets/partner-logo.svg`, **high** severity at 0.95 confidence, with two base64 rasters embedded inside an SVG. That's a materially worse asset problem than the one this PR introduces and it's already on main. Out of scope here, but worth a ticket while asset hygiene has someone's attention.
